Severe Flooding in Bangladesh Disrupts Automotive Supply Chains

Severe monsoon flooding in central Bangladesh has brought significant disruption to the country’s automotive industry, with several key manufacturing plants and transport routes affected. Industry officials and analysts warn that the ongoing inundation, which began late last week following days of torrential rain, could have lasting consequences for both domestic production and international supply chains.

The worst-affected areas include the Narayanganj and Gazipur districts, home to major component plants and assembly facilities. According to the Bangladesh Automotive Manufacturers Association (BAMA), at least four major factories have been forced to halt operations since Saturday due to floodwaters entering production floors and damaging equipment. “Our members are reporting extensive water damage to electrical systems and inventories,” BAMA Secretary-General Faridul Haque said in a statement Monday. “At this stage, we estimate a production loss of over 7,000 vehicles and thousands more in components.”

Local authorities have closed several highways and rail lines serving the Dhaka-Chattogram corridor, a vital artery for transporting automotive parts and finished vehicles to ports. Trucks carrying transmissions, chassis, and other key components are reportedly stranded, with some shipments delayed by more than 72 hours. “We are seeing significant congestion at logistics hubs, and the backlog is growing,” said Shahnaz Rahman, head of logistics at Rafiq Motors Ltd. “Some of our suppliers are warning of critical shortages if the situation does not improve within the next week.”

Analysts say the timing of the floods could worsen the industry’s recovery from recent global supply chain disruptions. “Automotive manufacturers in Bangladesh were just beginning to ramp up after a challenging year,” said Syed Zaman, an industry analyst at Dhaka-based research firm MarketPulse. “This flooding will set back production schedules and could impact export commitments, especially for firms supplying to Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.”

Union representatives have also raised concerns about worker safety and wage losses, as many employees have been unable to reach factories since Friday. “Hundreds of workers are stranded in their villages, while others are dealing with flooded homes,” said Mahmudul Islam, president of the National Auto Workers Union. “We urge employers to provide emergency support and ensure jobs are protected during this crisis.”

With water levels still rising in some low-lying industrial zones and rainfall forecasts remaining high, the full extent of the disruption is not yet clear. Both government and industry leaders are monitoring the situation closely, but restoration of normal operations is expected to take at least several more days.
